one_liner: Kernel-bypass runtime reallocating cores every 5 us; ZygOS-level tail latency, 6.3x Linux DNS throughput, idle cores freed for batch jobs.
what_it_does: Shenango is a C runtime plus a privileged daemon (iokerneld) for Linux servers that run latency-critical network services next to batch jobs. The IOKernel owns the NIC through DPDK, steers packets to each application, and grants or takes back cores; each application links libruntime.a and runs on lightweight user-level threads (uthreads) with blocking TCP/UDP calls (tcp_listen/tcp_accept/tcp_read/tcp_write, udp_listen, a per-datagram UDP spawner), plus mutexes, condvars, RCU and timers. It is not a drop-in: networked programs must be ported to its own socket API (the authors ported memcached and gdnsd), but a pthread shim lets unmodified pthread batch programs such as PARSEC run on it. There is no HTTP layer; thin C++ (rt::Thread, rt::Spawn with std::function) and Rust bindings wrap the C API.
how_it_is_fast: One busy-polling IOKernel core runs a congestion-detection check every 5 us: if any uthread or packet stays in a kthread's ring-buffer queue across two consecutive checks (current head vs previous tail, read from one shared cache line per kthread), the app gets one more core, and kthreads that find no work after local, hyperthread-sibling, random and all-kthread work stealing park and hand the core back. Cores are granted with eventfd wakeups plus sched_setaffinity and taken back with tgkill(SIGUSR1); a reallocation completes in 5.9 us, and the paper contrasts its 5 us balancing interval with 4 ms for Linux and 50 ms for Arachne. Inside the app, per-kthread runqueues with lock-free local wakeups, preallocated stacks, minimal register saves on cooperative yield, and stealing of packet/TCP processing across cores (dropping flow-consistent hashing, unlike ZygOS) keep scheduling cheap. Payloads are copied instead of zero-copy so Intel DDIO keeps packet buffers inside its LLC share.
when_to_use: A single-socket x86-64 server that runs a latency-critical request/response service (1-10 us service times, memcached- or RPC-like) next to batch work, where you need 99.9th-percentile latency under ~100 us and want idle cores to go to the batch job.
Load that jumps within microseconds (the paper tests 100k to 5M requests/s steps) where static kernel-bypass provisioning such as ZygOS or IX would have to keep all cores spinning for peak load.
High-rate small UDP request/response services on one 10 GbE port (gdnsd port: 5.7M vs 0.9M requests/s on Linux).
Research or reproduction of the NSDI'19 results, or as a readable reference for microsecond-scale core allocation (the whole congestion check and grant loop is about 80 lines in iokernel/cores.c).
You can give a full physical core (2 hyperthreads) to iokerneld, run it as root, and bind the NIC to DPDK.
when_not_to_use: Any new deployment: the maintainers mark it unmaintained and point to Caladan, which adds directpath (IOKernel off the datapath), TCP window scaling, user-interrupt time slicing and interference mitigations.
WAN, lossy or high bandwidth-delay paths: the from-scratch TCP stack has flow control and fast retransmit but no congestion control and no window scaling.

Peak throughput at very short service times (<2 us): the single IOKernel core caps out around 6.5M packets/s and becomes the bottleneck; ZygOS reaches higher peak memcached throughput (at worse latency).

Multi-socket/NUMA use, VMs, non-x86 CPUs, hosts without hyperthreading, or NICs other than the tested Intel 82599ES and Mellanox ConnectX-3 Pro (ConnectX-5 patches exist): the IOKernel only manages cores on package 0 and panics if hyperthreads are off unless built with CORES_NOHT; VM support is an unanswered issue.
You need HTTP, TLS or BSD-socket compatibility: none is provided, and existing servers must be rewritten against tcp_*/udp_* calls.

integration.dependencies: DPDK 19.11 as a git submodule with patched ixgbe/mlx4/mlx5 drivers (the paper used 18.11), libnuma, libdl, pthreads, 2 MB hugepages and System V shared memory (scripts/setup_machine.sh), a root-run iokerneld daemon; Mellanox OFED for Mellanox NICs; Rust bindings need bindgen 0.32 (clang) and a nightly toolchain
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with -std=gnu11 (runtime, IOKernel) and -std=gnu++11 (C++ bindings), -mssse3, -O3; no GCC version documented. Rust bindings use #![feature(llvm_asm)], which rustc nightly removed in January 2022, so a 2021 nightly is needed (issue #10 reports nightly-2021-06-06 works). Tested on Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.15.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux only; single socket (package 0); hyperthreading required by default; Intel 82599ES (ixgbe) or Mellanox ConnectX-3 Pro/ConnectX-5 via DPDK
integration.thread_safety: Built for multi-core use: uthreads migrate between kthreads via work stealing and the runtime supplies mutex, condvar and RCU. Blocking Linux syscalls are discouraged, and code must wrap thread-local accesses (including glibc malloc/free) in preempt_disable/preempt_enable because gcc caches TLS addresses across preemption; smalloc/sfree are the runtime's allocator.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the pthread shim (link libshim.a with -Wl,--wrap=main) runs unmodified pthread batch programs, but network services must be ported from Linux sockets or ZygOS's event API to Shenango's blocking tcp_*/udp_* calls and started under runtime_init with a config file

gotchas: TCP interop is limited: no window scaling (an mTCP client that assumed window scaling stalled because Shenango read its receive window as tiny, issue #6), no congestion control, and reader wakeups depend on the peer setting PSH or FIN.

Packet stealing and core changes reorder packets: under 0.07% arrive out of order with 1,200 connections and up to 3% with 24, with the runtime resequencing per socket under a lock (under 0.5% of cycles in the paper).

iokerneld pins itself to the first non-zero core of socket 0 and gives that core's hyperthread sibling to Linux and its control thread; running an app on a different NUMA node fails with 'base library per-thread init failed, ret = -12' (fix: numactl, issue #6), and setup_machine.sh reserves hugepages on node 0 only.
Not every primitive wins: in the paper's Table 2 an uncontended mutex costs 37 ns versus 30 ns for pthreads and 24 ns for Go; each uthread gets a 128 KB stack plus a 128 KB guard region.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Shenango over Demikernel or eRPC only when the goal is CPU efficiency, meaning microsecond-scale core reallocation among colocated apps behind a blocking-thread API, rather than the lowest per-request latency or RPC rate; for HTTP serving use Lwan or H2O, since Shenango has no HTTP layer. In practice, prefer its maintained successor Caladan.
verified_claims_summary: NSDI'19 paper, on one socket of a 12-core Xeon E5-2650v4 (all systems capped at 16 hyperthreads, 2 of them for the IOKernel) with an Intel 82599ES 10 GbE NIC, Ubuntu 18.04/kernel 4.15 and no compiler stated: memcached 1.5.6 (USR workload) next to PARSEC swaptions served over 5M requests/s at 37 us median and 93 us 99.9th percentile, about 1M requests/s more than ZygOS under the same latency bound, while leaving idle cycles to the batch job (ZygOS left none). Linux reached only ~0.8M requests/s even without batch work (and exceeded 2 ms 99.9th percentile at 0.4M with batch work), and ported gdnsd did 5.7M vs 0.9M UDP requests/s on Linux (6.33x).
status_note: Declared unmaintained by its authors (last code change 2021-03-25; README notice 2024-11-05) with Caladan as the active successor; Apache-2.0 (the unused ksched kernel module is GPL), so the code can be copied, but building it needs a patched DPDK 19.11 and a 2021 Rust nightly, which makes it research code, not a library to adopt.
